name: Pure Blue
lede: Pure Blue is an intense, slightly violet blue named in the xkcd color survey of 2010, and the phrase itself has a longer life as a description of blue pigments.

sections.title: A survey's idea of pure
sections.body:
Our library records this exact swatch from one source, the xkcd color survey of 2010, in which respondents named colors shown on screen [1]. It is a deep, saturated blue, leaning a little toward violet, with Medium Blue as its nearest standard name [1].

In plain speech *pure* means unmixed. The phrase also turns up as a pigment grade.

sections.title: Pure blue as a grade of azurite
sections.body:
The Pigment Compendium records that Chinese sources, following Yü, used "Flat blue" or "Pure blue" for the highest quality of azurite, the copper blue mineral [2]. It was sold under other names, Yunnan blue and Burmese blue, depending on where it was dug, and lower grades were Layered blue, Light blue and Granulated blue [2]. The same book says that Chinese barium copper silicate pigments sometimes formed pure blue or pure purple masses, though it is impossible to say whether this was intended [3].

An 1869 edition of Field's chromatography also mentions a cotton-seed blue, produced by a long chemical process until a very intense pure blue appeared, but Field adds that it was never introduced as a pigment [4].

sections.title: What the eye calls pure
sections.body: Vision has its own meaning. Livingstone explains that the eye registers a hue only when an opponent channel, red against green or blue against yellow, gives an unbalanced signal [5]. Ultramarine and cobalt blue both look like pure blues, even though cobalt reflects some green and some red light as well; the red cancels the cyan and leaves only the blue perception [5]. So a color can look pure while its spectrum is mixed. Related colors in the app are [[blue]], [[cobalt-blue]] and [[royal-blue]] and [[indigo]] [1].

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: No painting in our archive of 23,781 has this color covering at least 1 per cent of its canvas, within a color difference of 4, as photographed [6]. A paintings archive is a poor place to look for it, since this is a screen color [6]. In printed English the phrase peaks in the 1870s, and it rose in the 1850s [7]. The Google Books count includes every sense of the words, so it is a rough guide [7].
